title: What the simulator does
text:
What the simulator does.
Court of All Time compares two NBA team-seasons from any era, 1985–86 onward, and estimates how a single game between them would go on a neutral court. It gives a win chance for each team and a rough point margin. These matchups never happened, so the result is a model estimate for entertainment, not a forecast. The estimate comes from each team's full regular season: how well it scored and defended, and how often it won, each judged against the league it played in. (Source: the hist-v2 release manifest.)

title: Why teams are compared with their own league
text:
Why teams are compared with their own league.
Raw numbers drift a long way between eras. League offensive rating was about 105 to 108 points per 100 possessions in the late 1980s and 1990s, and about 115 in the 2020s. True shooting rose from about .530 to .580, and three-point attempts went from a small share of shots to about two in five. A model that read raw numbers would judge an older team on a scale that moved, and it would tilt evenly matched cross-era games toward modern teams. So the simulator reads each stat as a z-score: how many standard deviations a team was above or below the average of its own season's league. A team that was dominant for its time scores as dominant, whatever the era. (Source: reports/older_seasons_backtest.md.)

title: What a z-score means here
text:
What a z-score means here.
A z-score is the number of standard deviations a team's figure sits from the average of all teams in the same season. A net rating z of +2.0 means the team was two standard deviations better than an average team that season. Zero is exactly average. For defensive rating, opponent shooting and turnovers, a lower raw number is better, so the cards say "better" or "worse" rather than relying on the sign.

title: Neutral court
text:
Neutral court.
The underlying model was trained on real games, which have a home team. To make a fair cross-era matchup, the site scores each pairing twice, once with each team at home, and averages the two win chances. Neither team gets home-court advantage, and the two teams' chances always add up to 100%. The margin is neutralised the same way. (Source: scripts/export_static_site_data.py.)

title: What the simulator does not account for
text:
What the simulator does not account for.
The simulator sees full-season team averages only. It does not know about rosters, individual players, injuries, rest, trades during the season, playoff experience, coaching, rule changes beyond what shows up in the league averages, or how styles would match up. A team that changed a lot during the season is represented by its season-long average. It cannot say what would happen with different players, and it does not model individual stars.

title: Seasons before 1996–97
text:
Seasons before 1996–97.
The NBA's own advanced stats, such as offensive and defensive rating and pace, start in 1996–97. For the seasons from 1985–86 to 1995–96, the site computes them from the basic box score with the standard formulas. Where both exist, the formulas match the NBA's numbers closely: net rating is off by about 0.1 points per 100 possessions on average. Possessions are estimated with the usual formula, scaled to match the NBA's own counts. Rebound percentages cannot be rebuilt reliably, so they are not used for any season. (Source: reports/older_seasons_backtest.md.)

title: Season labels
text:
Season labels.
A season is named by both of its years, such as 1995–96, and keyed by the year it ended: the 1995–96 Chicago Bulls are `1996-bulls`, and "the '96 Bulls" means the same team. Team names are the ones the franchise used that season: the Seattle SuperSonics until 2007–08, the Washington Bullets until 1996–97, the New Jersey Nets until 2011–12, and so on. The 2019–20 Finals were played in October 2020 in the Orlando bubble, and they belong to the 2019–20 season.

title: Short seasons
text:
Short seasons.
Four seasons were shorter than 82 games: 1998–99 (50 games, after a lockout), 2011–12 (66 games, after a lockout), 2019–20 (stopped in March 2020 and finished in the bubble, so teams played between 64 and 75 games), and 2020–21 (72 games). Comparisons use win percentage, not raw wins, so those teams are not penalised. A short season is also noisier: a team's averages rest on fewer games.

title: The point margin
text:
The point margin.
Next to the win chance, the site shows a rough point margin from a separate ridge regression. It is approximate: on real games its typical error was about 11 points. It should be read as "about a two-possession game" or "a comfortable win", never as an exact score. The win chance and the margin come from different models, so they can disagree slightly. (Source: the hist-v2 release manifest.)

title: Series chances
text:
Series chances.
For a best-of-seven series, the site treats every game as an independent game at the same neutral-court win chance and adds up the ways a team can win four games first. A small edge in one game becomes a bigger edge over a series: a 60% single-game chance becomes about 71% over seven games. It ignores home court, adjustments between games, and injuries. (Source: frontend/src/lib/series.ts.)

title: Why the site publishes no accuracy figure
text:
Why the site publishes no accuracy figure.
A cross-era matchup never happened, so there is no real result to check it against. The model was checked on real games between teams of the same season, but that number would not tell a visitor how right a 1996 versus 2017 estimate is, and it invites the wrong comparison. The owner chose not to publish an accuracy figure for this release. An older version of the site once quoted a number that turned out to be inflated by a data error, and it must not be repeated. (Source: CONTRIBUTING.md, hist-v2 manifest.)

title: Where the data comes from
text:
Where the data comes from.
Team box scores and standings come from a public dataset of historical NBA games and box scores, published on Kaggle ("Historical NBA Data and Player Box Scores"). The site builds each team-season's regular-season and playoff profile from it. Champions are taken from the last playoff game of each season. Nothing on the site uses league or team logos or player images, and the site is not affiliated with the NBA or any team.

title: About the hist-v2 simulator
text:
About the hist-v2 simulator.
Neutral-court historical matchup simulator. Compares two completed NBA team-seasons (1985-86 onward), each measured against its own season's league rather than by raw numbers. An L1 logistic-regression classifier estimates the win probability; a ridge regressor gives a rough point margin. Output is a model estimate for entertainment, not a forecast or betting advice.

title: Limitations of the hist-v2 simulator
text:
Limitations of the hist-v2 simulator.
- Cross-era matchups never happened, so these outcomes cannot be validated against real results.
- Results are for a neutral court: each matchup is scored with both teams at home and the two averaged.
- Each team is compared with its own season's league: its stats are read as how far above or below that season's league average it was (a z-score), not as raw numbers, because scoring, shooting and pace changed between eras.
- In practice the model reads two numbers per team: its net rating and its win percentage, each against its own league. Every other stat it was offered carries zero weight.
- Seasons before 1996-97 use ratings, pace and shooting computed from the box score; the NBA's own advanced values exist only from 1996-97.
- Rebound percentages are not used: they cannot be rebuilt from the box score for older seasons.
- No accuracy figure is published for this release.
- The point margin is approximate; typical error on real games was about 11 points.
- Team strength comes from full-season averages, not rosters, injuries, or rest.

title: How the simulator weighs the two teams
text:
How the simulator weighs the two teams.
The hist-v2 classifier gives non-zero weight to 2 inputs: net rating and win %, each as a z-score against the team's own league. Every other stat it was offered carries zero weight.
With one team at home, the home team's log-odds of winning are 0.360 (home court) + 0.356 x (difference in net rating z-scores) + 0.129 x (difference in win % z-scores).
The site scores both home orders and averages the two probabilities, so neither team has home court.
One standard deviation of net rating moves the log-odds about 2.8 times as much as one standard deviation of win %, so net rating decides most matchups.
